segments.text: We're ready to get underway, and we have further
hearings on the Social Security
Amendment Bill. And the first submitter we have this afternoon is Good Shepherd New
Zealand. We have Good Shepherd New Zealand
online. Bree, over-
Kia ora
Oh, kia ora. Welcome. All right. We have
10 minutes with you this afternoon. The time is yours when you're ready to go.
Thank you, and thank you for the opportunity to speak today.
I'm the policy lead for Good Shepherd New Zealand.
We are a charitable NGO focused on two of the biggest issues facing
women and girls, in particular in New Zealand, being poverty and family violence,
and the challenges that stem from these.
First, I'll speak to the policy tightening eligibility criteria for jobseeker
support. So as noted in MSD's own RIS, the
benefits for young people of these changes are likely to be significantly
outweighed by the costs, and we're really concerned about the further hardship that
this may create for households. We do understand the need to target funding
towards those who most need it. But as the cost of living has risen, New
Zealand has seen more poverty and more of the squeezed middle, lower to
middle-income households who are struggling to make ends meet.
There is a serious risk that many families will not be able to financially support
their children past their school years.
As New Zealand is already experiencing high and unmoving child poverty rates
due to the financial pressures on households with children, these households are
also facing rising energy costs and food prices increasing, amongst
other things. Stagnant incomes at the moment are not sufficient
to meet these costs.
The Helen Clark Foundation's recent report on social cohesion found that one
in four New Zealand households go without meals because they can't afford food,
and the clients that we serve report similar activity.
The parental income limit in this policy, which is around $65,000 to
$67,000, is much lower than the annual gross
household income, which is currently sitting at around $139,000, and also
lower than some other parental income tests that we see for payments, such as the
student allowance, which is around $101,000 if you live with your
parents. It's currently unclear how family size and other dependents will be
taken into consideration here. What is clear is that young people
whose parents earn over this threshold but who will not or cannot support
them will be left behind. Rainbow youth and those experiencing family violence will
likely be over-represented in this group, especially where estrangement is
difficult to prove.
We note that the first two objectives in this policy, as noted in the bill, center
on fiscal sustainability and incentivizing youth to enter work.
But making it harder for young people to access the jobseeker benefit will not
incentivize them to enter a job market if there are no jobs to hire them.
The recent 2026 Salvation Army State of the Nation report states that over a
quarter of a million people are currently wanting work but are unable to find
it. That challenge is very real. The entry-level job market in
particular is challenged due to the rise of AI, the global economic
context, and many young people are applying for hundreds of jobs without
success. Under this policy, young people will also miss out on some of the
coaching and support that are offered by case managers through the jobseeker
benefit that might really be able to help them when applying for those roles.
We think that government policy should focus on investing in labor market
stimulus, increasing business activity, opportunities, and
education. MSD's original preferred option was
to provide a range of targeted employment and changing programs which predicted
savings in the long term through lower future benefit
levels. We do know that Budget 2026 has promised an
extra thousand Youth Guarantee places, which is great.
But given the policy in this bill is estimated to impact over
4,000 young people, there is a significant gap here.
We also know that unfortunately, many of the young people who are currently
struggling to find work are university graduates already, showing that
education alone is not currently sufficient to pull youth out of
unemployment. The job market needs to be stimulated as well to provide new
opportunities for those who are exiting tertiary education.
People also need funds to enable employment opportunities.
Young people who are denied benefits and have no money to buy a car
cannot travel to a job if public transport options don't exist.
They can't afford appropriate work wear for a job interview or buy tools needed for
their trade. They cannot pay for that additional training that could support them
into work. While the majority of the loans that we provide, so no
interest, no fee loans for people under a certain income threshold, they're usually
for things like a car or debt consolidation, we do also provide loans for
educational or training-related expenses or technology like laptops to
enable study. There is a need for these things.
If parents are forced to become financially responsible for their children for
longer, it's also likely that there'll be an increase in demand for assistance
provided by NGOs or charities like ourselves or food banks.
For example, the Zero Hunger Collective here at Kaikoore reports an increase in
two-income households who are visiting food banks across the country.
This is expected to only worsen. So that's in work poverty in
action. Charities and social services fill a really
needed gap in responses to poverty, but many have been forced to
close down due to funding cuts or contracts not being renewed.
The charitable sector can't be the ambulance at the bottom of the cliff, and we're
not going to succeed if there aren't contracts to fund them to do so.
I'll now move on to the second proposal in the Bill, changing the entry threshold
for the accommodation supplement.
We note that housing makes up a significant portion of financial
pressure for many households. Housing tends to be a fixed household
cost, so that's unable to be reduced or budgeted around.
While the majority of our clients are in rental or some form of
social housing, around 13% live in a home that they own
themselves. So this shows that despite owning their house, these
clients are under enough financial pressure to need to come to us to be able
to purchase those essential goods and services such as whiteware, for
example. Now, there is a number of reasons why people who own
homes may be experiencing financial stress.
Even though we have seen some house price trend improvement and some shifts
in the affordability criteria, which is fantastic, those who
bought homes at record highs or are locked in those higher interest
rates will continue to struggle.
Local government rates across the country are also set to increase 5% to
10% in the coming year. High numbers of redundancies
across all sectors, public, private, and social sector,
seriously reduce household incomes, especially in this really tough
job market we're currently in, where unemployment might be extended.
Divorce or separation can result in one person taking over a mortgage
unexpectedly, and this is particularly challenging when family violence is
involved. Both situations disproportionately impact women's
financial wellbeing. Simply stating that the accommodation supplement
exists to help homeowners accumulate a personal asset
ignores the current state of the economy and the variable housing market.
I'll share a quick example of a Good Shepherd client who I'll call Lillian.
Lillian had experienced family violence in her relationship with her ex-husband.
When he left, she suddenly found herself to be a solo mum living in the
house that they legally co-owned together, but he'd stopped paying the mortgage,
maintenance for the house, any other bills.
The washing machine broke, the shower leaked, but she couldn't afford to fix them.
While trying to get her life back together after abuse, she had to navigate paying
these bills alone on a limited budget.
With our help, she was eventually supported into financial stability, but this
example shows some of the complexity of homeowner situations and how
it's often a lot more complicated than that.
So if this Bill goes through, we do really strongly support
the exclusions that are noted, especially for superannuants.
Our own research into single older women's housing needs has shown
that many older people who own their home do not experience
affordable, warm housing. Poor housing quality, particularly
for older homes that were purchased potentially many decades ago,
combined with rising rates and insurance costs, put significant pressure on
superannuant homeowners who lack the ability to generate additional
income. Just another client example I'll share.
We have recently supported an 80-year-old woman living in rural
South Island, so the deep south. Her house was purchased
many decades ago, and she couldn't afford to upkeep it.
Her health was really suffering because the heating was completely inadequate
during the freezing winters. Her family lived far away, and she was
reliant completely on the super. Her budget was really tight, and she couldn't
afford to buy a heat pump. So we were able to support her by providing a grant, and
we've helped many others like her with this kind of essential home maintenance
needs. But this shows how older people are desperately in need of any
dollar that they are able to get, especially because they can't
earn the additional income.
So overall, we are disappointed to see another policy progressing that's
focused on these short-term financial savings instead of long-term
outcomes. We believe that kicking the can down the road does not
support financial sustainability in the long run.
It just creates false economies, and we need to take a long-term
lens. Thank you for your time.
Thank you. Any questions, members?

paper, we call these supports as imagined,

As I mentioned, barriers to employment include inaccessible

the need for workplace accommodations, limited availability of
specialist employment support, and disrupted education pathways.
Job seeker can act as a stabilizing support

extra challenge and does exhaust our young people sometimes.
So sometimes they need a bit of time to recover as they prepare to seek

This gives them time to explore rehabilitation options, disability-related

And this is where the other stuff gets interesting, because part-time

and it can be really difficult to navigate this

barriers to financial support without addressing the underlying

makes it harder to achieve independence.

Families with a disabled child are more likely to experience material

more likely to report unmet health and disability-related needs,

This means that these households are less able to provide financial

period where they need more support.
More support to navigate the options, more support to navigate

For our young people, income support is the foundation that allows them to

It helps with the support and assistive technology.

If they want to undertake volunteer work or to

work, that comes with costs.
So reducing access to income support before employment barriers are addressed
makes the pathway into employment harder, not
easier. And lastly, we're also concerned about the
proposed changes around the accommodation supplement,
and that is because
of those income-related challenges, and it's really important,
